newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bonn raises deficit forecast close to ceiling.
newsitem.headline: Bonn raises deficit forecast close to ceiling.

text.p: Germany has raised its forecast for this year's budget deficit to 2.9 percent of gross domestic product, only just below the three percent Maastricht Treaty ceiling for joining a single European currency, the government's annual economic report said.

The report, due to be reviewed by Chancellor Helmut Kohl's cabinet on Tuesday, showed pressures from the jobs market had forced an upward revision in the deficit forecast from the 2.5 percent scenario on which Finance Minister Theo Waigel's 1997 budget was based, leaving precious little room for manoeuvre.
German unemployment, set to hit new post-war records this winter, could fall below four million later this year but only if there is a sustained rebound in domestic demand, it said.

The country's unemployment crisis was "an enormous challenge", said a draft of the report obtained by Reuters, but it would not knock Germany off its course of qualifying for European economic and monetary union in 1999.
"All those whose decisions and actions have an impact on economic events must make their contribution to improve the jobs market situation. They all bear responsibility," it said.
Most key data from the report, obtained by Reuters, have already been leaked, but the deficit figure which economists and financial markets have been looking for was buried on page 87.
The report, drafted by experts from Guenter Rexrodt's Economics Ministry, still showed a significant decline in the budget deficit from the 3.9 percent of GDP figure last year
It reiterated Germany's tough position on adherence to the deficit goal this year to ensure that European monetary union, planned for 1999, had solid foundations.
"Stable money in the European single market and a robust international value of the single currency are important preconditions for investment, jobs and growth," it said.
"For these, strict observance of the convergence criteria and sustained financial solidity are vital."
The report also predicted economic growth of 2.5 percent this year, with recovery borne by rapid export growth.
Inflation will stay low at 1.5 percent, but the jobless rate will climb to 11 percent -- equivalent to 4.1 million unemployed -- from 10.3 percent in 1996.
The report, which runs to more than 100 pages, urged Germany to tackle the structural impediments which have held up job creation.
Ursula Engelen-Kefer, deputy head of the DGB trade union movement, on Monday predicted unemployment would climb to 4.5 million in February, the highest since World War Two.
Outlining the government's 10-point strategy of "reforms for jobs", the report said state spending should be cut back from around 50 percent of GDP to the pre-unification level of 46 percent by 2000.

Left open, however, was the question of restructuring the social security system. In addition to big tax cuts announced by the Bonn coalition last week, Labour Minister Norbert Bluem was putting final touches to a pensions reform plan on Monday.

The report also said that Germany should force the pace of privatisation to slim down its economic interests. Provincial states and municipalities have lagged behind progress made by the Bonn government in recent years.
And the report also called for greater efforts to bring former communist eastern Germany's productive potential in line with its demand for goods.

The east, after a post-unification boom, has lost its economic dynamism. Self-sustaining growth remains out of reach, due to a lack of competitiveness. A decision on granting more economic aid after 1998 will be taken this spring, it said.

In an initial reaction, German industry association (BDI) welcomed the report's emphasis on the need for faster growth to create jobs, but said planned tax reforms must lighten the burden on companies to boost job creation.
"This can only happen when Germany's structural weaknesses are removed," the BDI said in a statement. "The government's 10 points go in the right direction."
